chapterBreakdown.gentle:
After the stretch stories, the book widens the frame and asks what kind of system can carry strong performance over time. That is why Chapter 15 matters. It introduces continuous performance management and CFRs to show that OKRs do not work best in isolation.

The first lesson in the chapter is that goals need a broader support system around them. OKRs can define direction and ambition, but performance becomes stronger when people also have ongoing conversation, feedback, and recognition. That is the role CFRs play here. They make the management system more continuous instead of leaving everything to periodic evaluation.

The chapter also makes a direct contrast with static annual-review logic. A periodic judgment can capture a moment, but it is weaker than useful conversation and feedback that happen while the work is still alive. Ongoing support helps people sustain, discuss, and improve performance instead of waiting too long to interpret it.

The chapter protects an important limit at the same time. Continuous performance management is not endless judgment or constant pressure. The stronger point is not more surveillance. It is that support around performance becomes steadier, more useful, and more connected to real work over time.

The durable lesson is that OKRs and CFRs belong together inside a broader system of continuous performance management. That is the chapter's real transition into Part 2. Once that system is clear, the book can move into the Adobe story and show what leaving annual reviews behind looks like in practice.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Part 2 widens from the stretch sequence into the larger system that has to carry performance over time. That is why it introduces continuous performance management and CFRs. The chapter argues that OKRs work best inside an ongoing framework of conversation, feedback, and recognition rather than as a stand-alone goal method.

The first hard distinction is that goals are not enough by themselves. OKRs define direction, but performance is stronger when useful conversation happens more often, feedback arrives closer to the work, and recognition reinforces progress while people can still learn from it. CFRs therefore add the continuous support layer around the goal system.

The chapter contrasts this with static annual-review logic. A periodic judgment can still matter, but it is weaker than ongoing support that helps people adjust while the work is still alive. Delayed evaluation is too narrow and too late to carry the full burden of performance management by itself.

It also rejects a flattering counterfeit. Continuous performance management does not mean nonstop surveillance or endless judgment theater. The stronger claim is that support becomes more continuous and more useful, not merely more frequent and louder.

The durable lesson is that OKRs and CFRs belong together inside a broader system of continuous performance management. That is what makes Chapter 15 the hinge into Part 2. Once the system is established conceptually, the Adobe story can test what it looks like in a named company case.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Stretch proved what ambitious goals can do. Chapter 15 asks what system can keep that performance alive. That is why it introduces continuous performance management and CFRs. The chapter matters because it says goals alone are strategically incomplete.

The first chapter distinction is severe. OKRs can define direction, but they cannot carry the whole management burden by themselves. Performance gets stronger when conversation, feedback, and recognition stay alive around the work instead of being trapped inside occasional evaluations. CFRs supply that live support layer.

The chapter also cuts against static annual-review logic. A delayed verdict is weaker than a live system that helps people discuss, improve, and sustain performance while the work is still moving. Annual review logic can capture a moment, but it is too blunt to do all the work Part 2 now asks of management.

The chapter rejects the fake hard answer at the same time. Continuous management is not constant pressure theater. More surveillance is weaker than better support. The system matters because the signals become more useful, not because the scrutiny gets louder.

So the real lesson is exact. OKRs and CFRs belong together inside a broader continuous performance system. That is what opens Part 2. Once that system is clear, the book can move into Adobe and test what leaving annual reviews behind looks like under real conditions.
